quick: 5 mg/kg up to 300 mg once daily (treatment)
Take on an empty stomach - food reduces absorption
Use for active TB; benefit justifies risk (Category C)
Compatible; low milk levels (give infant pyridoxine)
Usually no change; caution in severe impairment
Avoid in acute liver disease; monitor LFTs
summary: Isoniazid (INH) is a first-line bactericidal antitubercular drug used for all susceptible forms of tuberculosis (always with other agents for active disease) and for latent TB prevention. Adult treatment dose is 5 mg/kg up to 300 mg daily. It carries a boxed warning for severe and sometimes fatal hepatitis, the risk of which rises with age and alcohol use. Pyridoxine is given to prevent peripheral neuropathy.
indications: Treatment of all forms of tuberculosis caused by susceptible organisms (in combination for active disease)
Preventive (latent TB) therapy in high-risk groups regardless of age (e.g., HIV infection, close contacts, recent converters)

dosage.d: 5 mg/kg up to 300 mg daily in a single dose
dosage.n: Always combine with other anti-TB drugs

dosage.d: 15 mg/kg up to 900 mg, 2-3 times per week

dosage.n: Prevents peripheral neuropathy in at-risk patients

admin: Take orally on an empty stomach, 1 hour before or 2 hours after meals
Do not take with food - bioavailability is significantly reduced
Avoid tyramine-rich (cheese, red wine) and histamine-rich (some fish) foods
Co-administer pyridoxine in malnourished, diabetic, alcoholic, pregnant or HIV patients
Never use as single-drug therapy for active tuberculosis
moa: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by the mycobacterial catalase-peroxidase KatG. The activated form inhibits the enzymes (InhA) involved in synthesis of mycolic acids, essential components of the mycobacterial cell wall. At therapeutic levels it is bactericidal against actively dividing intracellular and extracellular Mycobacterium tuberculosis.

absolute: Previous isoniazid-associated hepatic injury or drug-induced hepatitis
Severe hypersensitivity reactions (drug fever, chills, arthritis) to isoniazid
Acute liver disease of any cause
monitor: Signs of hepatitis (anorexia, nausea, fatigue, jaundice)

preg: Pregnancy Category C. Isoniazid crosses the placenta. It should be used to treat active tuberculosis in pregnancy because benefit justifies the potential risk; preventive therapy is generally deferred until after delivery. Give pyridoxine and observe the neonate.
lact: Concentrations in breast milk are small and do not produce toxicity in the nursing infant, so breastfeeding need not be discouraged; however milk levels are too low to treat or prevent TB in the infant. Give the breastfed infant supplemental pyridoxine.
renal: Usually no dosage change is needed because isoniazid is metabolized by the liver. Use caution in severe renal impairment, particularly in slow acetylators, and monitor for cerebellar syndrome and neurotoxicity.
hepatic: Boxed warning for severe, sometimes fatal hepatitis, risk rising with age and alcohol. Contraindicated in acute liver disease and prior INH hepatic injury. Check baseline AST/ALT (especially age >=35) and monitor; stop if transaminases rise markedly or symptoms of hepatitis appear.

major: Acetaminophen - increased hepatotoxicity via CYP2E1 induction
Carbamazepine and phenytoin - isoniazid inhibits metabolism causing toxicity
Hepatotoxic drugs / rifampin - additive liver injury
moderate: Tyramine-containing foods - MAO inhibition can cause hypertensive/flushing reaction
interactions.food: Take on an empty stomach; food lowers absorption. Avoid tyramine-rich (aged cheese, red wine) and histamine-rich foods (some tropical fish) to prevent flushing, headache and palpitations.
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - daily use markedly increases the risk of isoniazid hepatitis.
interactions.diagnostics: Can raise AST/ALT and bilirubin; may cause false-positive urine glucose with copper reduction tests; can lower pyridoxine levels.

serious: Severe cutaneous reactions (SJS, TEN, DRESS, AGEP)

monitoring: Baseline and periodic AST/ALT, especially in patients aged 35 and older
Monthly clinical review for symptoms of hepatitis
Visual symptoms (optic neuritis) and signs of cerebellar dysfunction
counsel: Take on an empty stomach, away from food and antacids
Stop and report at once if you develop nausea, loss of appetite, dark urine, yellow skin/eyes or right-sided tummy pain
Report tingling or numbness in hands or feet - you may need vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
Take every dose as scheduled and complete the full course to prevent resistance
pk: Bactericidal activity from start of therapy
Plasma peak about 1-2 hours after an oral dose
Fast acetylators ~0.5-1.6 h; slow acetylators ~2-5 h
Store at 20-25 C (68-77 F) in a tight container
pearls: Boxed warning: severe/fatal hepatitis - risk increases with age (>=35) and daily alcohol; monitor LFTs and symptoms
Always combine with other agents for active TB; single-drug therapy breeds resistance
Give pyridoxine 10-25 mg/day to prevent peripheral neuropathy in at-risk patients
Acetylator status (fast vs slow) affects half-life and toxicity
Overdose triad: refractory seizures, metabolic acidosis and coma - treat with high-dose IV pyridoxine
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed one and resume the schedule - do not double up. Try not to miss doses, as interruptions promote drug resistance.
overdose: Overdose causes nausea, vomiting, slurred speech, the classic triad of refractory seizures, severe metabolic acidosis and coma, plus hyperglycemia. Treatment: secure airway, give intravenous pyridoxine gram-for-gram with the ingested isoniazid dose (or 5 g empirically if amount unknown), control seizures with benzodiazepines, correct acidosis, and consider activated charcoal/hemodialysis.
